title: Satguru Guru Nanak's Blessings (Being a ruler of Khorasan (Babur) Threatened India) The Minister's Counsel

blocks.text: Chaupai:

India being a land of great spiritual saints, They would certainly lend their support to India's sovereign. How could Babur 's forces conquer the Indian emperor, If the spiritual saints bestowed their blessings on him. (1)
lines: India being a land of great spiritual saints,
They would certainly lend their support to India's sovereign.
How could Babur 's forces conquer the Indian emperor,
If the spiritual saints bestowed their blessings on him.

blocks.text: There happened to be a Hindu spiritual saint, Who excelled himself in spirituality among all the saints. As no other saint could be as perfect as he in piety, Any rival who confronted him got vanquished in spiritual debate. (2)
lines: There happened to be a Hindu spiritual saint,
Who excelled himself in spirituality among all the saints.
As no other saint could be as perfect as he in piety,
Any rival who confronted him got vanquished in spiritual debate.

blocks.text: Both the Hindus and the Muslims, being born from the same source, He (Guru Nanak) considered both equally worthy of his grace. So being revered by both the communities, Both Hindus and Muslims remained keen to receive his blessings. (3)
lines: Both the Hindus and the Muslims, being born from the same source,
He (Guru Nanak) considered both equally worthy of his grace.
So being revered by both the communities,
Both Hindus and Muslims remained keen to receive his blessings.

blocks.text: So, perfect was he in his spiritual dispensation, As if he was eternally in communication with the Divine. He (the minister) himself had confirmed Guru Nanak's divinity, As everything that Nanak predicted came out to be true. (4)
lines: So, perfect was he in his spiritual dispensation,
As if he was eternally in communication with the Divine.
He (the minister) himself had confirmed Guru Nanak's divinity,
As everything that Nanak predicted came out to be true.

blocks.text: Dohra:

The minister advised Babur to seek Guru Nanak's permission, If the latter wanted to bring India under his occupation. He must, under no circumstance, set foot in India, Without getting clearance from Guru Nanak for his mission. (5)
lines: The minister advised Babur to seek Guru Nanak's permission,
If the latter wanted to bring India under his occupation.
He must, under no circumstance, set foot in India,
Without getting clearance from Guru Nanak for his mission.

blocks.text: Chaupai:

Hearing this argument, did Daulat Khan speak, That he himself accepted Nanak as his spiritual mentor. Since he had proceeded to Kabul on Guru's instructions, He advised Babur to seek Guru Nanak's permission as well. (6)
lines: Hearing this argument, did Daulat Khan speak,
That he himself accepted Nanak as his spiritual mentor.
Since he had proceeded to Kabul on Guru's instructions,
He advised Babur to seek Guru Nanak's permission as well.

blocks.text: He (Daulat Khan) had proceeded to Kabul after Guru's prophetic utterance, That Lodhi Pathans would stand divested of sovereignty. It was after Guru Nanak had promised to bless the Mughals with sovereignty, That Daulat Khan had proceeded on his way to Kabul. (7)
lines: He (Daulat Khan) had proceeded to Kabul after Guru's prophetic utterance,
That Lodhi Pathans would stand divested of sovereignty.
It was after Guru Nanak had promised to bless the Mughals with sovereignty,
That Daulat Khan had proceeded on his way to Kabul.

blocks.text: At this, Babul (in his bigoted arrogance) made a remark: Who was Nanak to bestow sovereignty on the Mughals? The Mughals would receive sovereignty from their own prophet, Who occupied a hallowed place in the Divine Court. (8)
lines: At this,
Babul (in his bigoted arrogance) made a remark: Who was Nanak to bestow sovereignty on the Mughals?
The Mughals would receive sovereignty from their own prophet,
Who occupied a hallowed place in the Divine Court.

blocks.text: The Mughals would get their aspirations fulfilled from their own prophet, As the latter was as powerful in divinity as God. He (Babur) himself would see Nanak with his own eyes, Whether the latter was really worthy of reposing one's trust. (9)
lines: The Mughals would get their aspirations fulfilled from their own prophet,
As the latter was as powerful in divinity as God.
He (Babur) himself would see Nanak with his own eyes,
Whether the latter was really worthy of reposing one's trust.

blocks.text: Dohra:

In response to Babur's apprehensions, Daulat Khan remarked, That Guru Nanak was a beloved Hindu prophet of the Divine. Daulat Khan entreated Babur to proceed to see Guru Nanak, So that he might feel assured of Guru Nanak's divinity. (10)
lines: In response to Babur's apprehensions,
Daulat Khan remarked,
That Guru Nanak was a beloved Hindu prophet of the Divine.
Daulat Khan entreated Babur to proceed to see Guru Nanak,
So that he might feel assured of Guru Nanak's divinity.

blocks.text: Chaupai:

Countering Daulat Khan's remarks, Babur remonstrated: What if the Hindu prophet failed to be worthy of his trust? In that case, he (Babur) would punish that Hindu prophet, Burying him alive in the earth after converting him to Islam. (11)
lines: Countering Daulat Khan's remarks,
Babur remonstrated: What if the Hindu prophet failed to be worthy of his trust?
In that case, he (Babur) would punish that Hindu prophet,
Burying him alive in the earth after converting him to Islam.

blocks.text: Being a fake/counterfeit prophet, he would take to his heels, As all the Hindus were scared of Babur's very name. Definitely would he run for his life in scarce of Babur, To seek shelter in the mountains in the higher regions. (12)
lines: Being a fake/counterfeit prophet, he would take to his heels,
As all the Hindus were scared of Babur's very name.
Definitely would he run for his life in scarce of Babur,
To seek shelter in the mountains in the higher regions.

blocks.text: Never would he desert if he be a genuine prophet, Certainly would he escape if he be a counterfeit. Himself would he (Babur) judge if the latter be real or fake, Whether he was an imposter or a genuine prophet. (13)
lines: Never would he desert if he be a genuine prophet,
Certainly would he escape if he be a counterfeit.
Himself would he (Babur) judge if the latter be real or fake,
Whether he was an imposter or a genuine prophet.

blocks.text: Sortha:
Making Daulat Rai as his guide from Kabul, Babur led an expedition to conquer India. At that moment, the Guru uttered to the accompaniment of music, The following hymn from his sacred lips: (14)
lines: Making Daulat Rai as his guide from Kabul,
Babur led an expedition to conquer India.
At that moment, the Guru uttered to the accompaniment of music,
The following hymn from his sacred lips:

blocks.text: Guru Granth Sahib:
Shabad:
Handing over Khorasan's1 governance to another, The invading Babur terrorized the people of India.
The creator, not taking the blame (for decimating the Pathans) upon Himself, Willed the Mughals to launch an invasion on India.
Chaupai:

Asking Daulat Khan to guide the Mughal troops towards India, Babur kept on entrusting the enroute territory after getting a ransom. Thereafter, he ransacked a village occupied by Pathan residents, Which was known by the name Saidpur2 at that time. (15)
lines: Asking Daulat Khan to guide the Mughal troops towards India,
Babur kept on entrusting the enroute territory after getting a ransom.
Thereafter, he ransacked a village occupied by Pathan residents,
Which was known by the name Saidpur2 at that time.

blocks.text: For having shown disrespect to Guru Nanak once, The residents of this village had to bear this devastation. Thereafter, summoning Daulat Khan to his own camp, Babur issued orders to him to the following effect: (16)
lines: For having shown disrespect to Guru Nanak once,
The residents of this village had to bear this devastation.
Thereafter, summoning Daulat Khan to his own camp,
Babur issued orders to him to the following effect:

blocks.text: Since his (Babur's) forces had reached near Punjab, Nanak's own country, Nanak's seat had been reported to be near Emnabad. Was Nanak still at his own seat or had he made good his escape, Scared out of his wits by the approach of Mughal troops? (17)
lines: Since his (Babur's) forces had reached near Punjab,
Nanak's own country,
Nanak's seat had been reported to be near Emnabad.
Was Nanak still at his own seat or had he made good his escape,
Scared out of his wits by the approach of Mughal troops?

blocks.text: Ordering Daulat Khan to bring Nanak back if he had escaped, And ask Nanak to enter into negotiations with him (Babur). Assuring Daulat Khan of not ill-treating Nanak in anyway, Babur offered to dole out landed property to Nanak if he so desired. (18)
lines: Ordering Daulat Khan to bring Nanak back if he had escaped,
And ask Nanak to enter into negotiations with him (Babur).
Assuring Daulat Khan of not ill-treating Nanak in anyway,
Babur offered to dole out landed property to Nanak if he so desired.

blocks.text: Babur, being nit-witted idiot, could never realize, That no scare of any kind could unnerve the great Guru. The Guru, being the creator and destroyer of the whole world, The whole universe prospered under the command of his Divine Will. (19)
lines: Babur, being nit-witted idiot, could never realize,
That no scare of any kind could unnerve the great Guru.
The Guru, being the creator and destroyer of the whole world,
The whole universe prospered under the command of his Divine Will.

blocks.text: Dohra:

The spot where Guru Nanak sat in deep meditation, Was situated upon a mound of hard rocks and pebbles. So immovable remained Guru's seat that it never shook, Even if the whole earth and mountains shook and quaked. (20)
lines: The spot where Guru Nanak sat in deep meditation,
Was situated upon a mound of hard rocks and pebbles.
So immovable remained Guru's seat that it never shook,
Even if the whole earth and mountains shook and quaked.

blocks.text: Chaupai:

Having received verbal orders from Babur, Daulat Khan proceeded posthaste towards Guru's seat. Spotting out the Guru's seat after arriving in its vicinity, He started walking on foot after dismounting from his steed. (21)
lines: Having received verbal orders from Babur,
Daulat Khan proceeded posthaste towards Guru's seat.
Spotting out the Guru's seat after arriving in its vicinity,
He started walking on foot after dismounting from his steed.

blocks.text: Bowing his head and paying obeisance from a distance, Daulat placed his head at the lotus feet of Guru Nanak. Having remained prostrated at the Guru's feet for long, The great Guru asked Daulat Khan to rise from the ground. (22)
lines: Bowing his head and paying obeisance from a distance,
Daulat placed his head at the lotus feet of Guru Nanak.
Having remained prostrated at the Guru's feet for long,
The great Guru asked Daulat Khan to rise from the ground.

blocks.text: Even though the Guru being omniscient of all developments, The Guru let Daulat Khan narrate the whole situation. Having narrated all the developments of the past, Daulat Khan conveyed Babur's wish to meet the Guru. (23)
lines: Even though the Guru being omniscient of all developments,
The Guru let Daulat Khan narrate the whole situation.
Having narrated all the developments of the past,
Daulat Khan conveyed Babur's wish to meet the Guru.

blocks.text: The great Guru offered to march himself to Babur's camp, As Babur's armed bands would disturb the people's peace. The Guru himself would go to know Babur's intentions, And gauge what Babur contemplated in his mind. (24)
lines: The great Guru offered to march himself to Babur's camp,
As Babur's armed bands would disturb the people's peace.
The Guru himself would go to know Babur's intentions,
And gauge what Babur contemplated in his mind.

blocks.text: Dohra:

The great Guru, Guru Nanak soon arrived at a place, Where Babur was putting up in a camp. Thereupon, the Guru asked Mardana, his companion, That he should strike a melody on his stringed instrument. (25)
lines: The great Guru,
Guru Nanak soon arrived at a place,
Where Babur was putting up in a camp.
Thereupon, the Guru asked Mardana, his companion,
That he should strike a melody on his stringed instrument.

blocks.text: Chaupai:

As Mardana struck a melodious tune on his Rabab3 , The Mughal troops rushed to listen to this fascinating music. Having heard the spiritual melody, Babur felt, That Guru Nanak himself had arrived at his army camp. (26)
lines: As Mardana struck a melodious tune on his Rabab3 ,
The Mughal troops rushed to listen to this fascinating music.
Having heard the spiritual melody,
Babur felt,
That Guru Nanak himself had arrived at his army camp.

blocks.text: As Daulat Khan brought information about Guru Nanak's arrival, Babur felt assured about Guru Nanak's Divinity. Thereafter, calling for his royal mode of conveyance, Babur wished to pay a visit to Guru Nanak himself. (27)
lines: As Daulat Khan brought information about Guru Nanak's arrival,
Babur felt assured about Guru Nanak's Divinity.
Thereafter, calling for his royal mode of conveyance,
Babur wished to pay a visit to Guru Nanak himself.

blocks.text: (Before proceeding) Babur enquired from Daulat Khan, What kind of offering should Babur place before Guru Nanak. Daulat Khan informed Babur the Guru needed no offerings, As all the people received their cherished boons from Nanak. (28)
lines: (Before proceeding) Babur enquired from Daulat Khan,
What kind of offering should Babur place before Guru Nanak.
Daulat Khan informed Babur the Guru needed no offerings,
As all the people received their cherished boons from Nanak.

blocks.text: All temporal and spiritual powers were vested in Guru Nanak, As Babur himself would observe after his arrival there. Thereupon, Babur informed his companion Daulat Khan, that, It behoved not a royal personage to approach a saint empty-handed. (29)
lines: All temporal and spiritual powers were vested in Guru Nanak,
As Babur himself would observe after his arrival there.
Thereupon,
Babur informed his companion Daulat Khan, that,
It behoved not a royal personage to approach a saint empty-handed.

blocks.text: Dohra:
Never should one ever go empty-handed, On a visit to a mendicant, a monarch, and one's teacher. One is bound to fail in getting their blessings, Without placing a (token) offering before them. (30)
lines: Never should one ever go empty-handed,
On a visit to a mendicant, a monarch, and one's teacher.
One is bound to fail in getting their blessings,
Without placing a (token) offering before them.

blocks.text: Chaupai:

Upon this, advising Babur to make an offering of cannabis, Daulat Khan asked Babur to place it before the Guru. Thereafter, carrying a bag full of cannabis leaves, Babur placed it before the Guru after dismounting from a horse. (31)
lines: Upon this, advising Babur to make an offering of cannabis,
Daulat Khan asked Babur to place it before the Guru.
Thereafter, carrying a bag full of cannabis leaves,
Babur placed it before the Guru after dismounting from a horse.

blocks.text: Thereafter the Guru, after according due honour to the Mughal ruler, Asked him the reasons for being cross with him (Nanak). The Guru told Babur that he never obstructed Babur's advance, As he (the Guru) had been all long sitting on that rocky seat. (32)
lines: Thereafter the Guru, after according due honour to the Mughal ruler,
Asked him the reasons for being cross with him (Nanak).
The Guru told Babur that he never obstructed Babur's advance,
As he (the Guru) had been all long sitting on that rocky seat.

blocks.text: The Guru asked Babur to mete out any punishment to the former, As he had been contemplating at the time of his departure. Babur was free to allay his apprehensions that he had, Whether Guru Nanak was a fake or a genuine prophet. (33)
lines: The Guru asked Babur to mete out any punishment to the former,
As he had been contemplating at the time of his departure.
Babur was free to allay his apprehensions that he had,
Whether Guru Nanak was a fake or a genuine prophet.

blocks.text: He must confirm if Nanak followed path of truth or falsehood, The Guru was willing to offer himself for a close scrutiny. Found genuine, Babur could acknowledge Guru Nanak as a spiritual prophet, Found fake, he was free to get the Guru slaughtered. (34)
lines: He must confirm if Nanak followed path of truth or falsehood,
The Guru was willing to offer himself for a close scrutiny.
Found genuine,
Babur could acknowledge Guru Nanak as a spiritual prophet,
Found fake, he was free to get the Guru slaughtered.

blocks.text: Dohra:
Truth resides and rests with the Divine Lord, Elsewhere it is never found and observed. The temporal monarchs and rulers of kingdoms, Have all been putting spiritual prophets to test. (35)
lines: Truth resides and rests with the Divine Lord,
Elsewhere it is never found and observed.
The temporal monarchs and rulers of kingdoms,
Have all been putting spiritual prophets to test.

blocks.text: As Babur wished the Guru to workout some miracles, The Guru would loath to display any such feats. Display of miraculous feats not only invited Divine wrath, These also alienated the spiritual saints from the Divine as well. (36)
lines: As Babur wished the Guru to workout some miracles,
The Guru would loath to display any such feats.
Display of miraculous feats not only invited Divine wrath,
These also alienated the spiritual saints from the Divine as well.

blocks.text: Chaupai:

If any prophet claimed to work out miracles, Why could such a prophet not become a monarch as well? Power of working out miracles vested in the Divine Lord, alone, For which people accepted Him as the Supreme God. (37)
lines: If any prophet claimed to work out miracles,
Why could such a prophet not become a monarch as well?
Power of working out miracles vested in the Divine Lord, alone,
For which people accepted Him as the Supreme God.

blocks.text: Whosoever displays any miracles while being a human being, He is terribly harassed by the people of this world. Whosoever lives in intimate communication with God, He always shuns the temptation to work out miracles. (38)
lines: Whosoever displays any miracles while being a human being,
He is terribly harassed by the people of this world.
Whosoever lives in intimate communication with God,
He always shuns the temptation to work out miracles.

blocks.text: As Babur was too keen to see demonstration of miracles, It was not a morally justifiable act on his part. Very often, miracles workout in two diverse ways, Either resulting in blessings or ending up in disasters. (39)
lines: As Babur was too keen to see demonstration of miracles,
It was not a morally justifiable act on his part.
Very often, miracles workout in two diverse ways,
Either resulting in blessings or ending up in disasters.

blocks.text: While serving with devotion saints bring out their blessings, Insisting upon them to show miracles brings out their curse. Blessings and curses both work out as miracles, While alienating a spiritual prophet from the Divine Lord. (40)
lines: While serving with devotion saints bring out their blessings,
Insisting upon them to show miracles brings out their curse.
Blessings and curses both work out as miracles,
While alienating a spiritual prophet from the Divine Lord.

blocks.text: Dohra:

Cursed miracles are the fancy of temporal monarchs, Who seize others' belonging with coercion and duress. If ever a saint indulges in working out miracles, He is sure to find himself alienated from the Divine. (41)
lines: Cursed miracles are the fancy of temporal monarchs,
Who seize others' belonging with coercion and duress.
If ever a saint indulges in working out miracles,
He is sure to find himself alienated from the Divine.

blocks.text: Upon this, Babur realized Guru Nanak's omniscience, Since the Guru had laid bare all Babur's secret thoughts. He decided to share all his fears and aspirations, After he felt assured about Guru Nanak's omniscience. (42)
lines: Upon this,
Babur realized Guru Nanak's omniscience,
Since the Guru had laid bare all Babur's secret thoughts.
He decided to share all his fears and aspirations,
After he felt assured about Guru Nanak's omniscience.

blocks.text: Chaupai:

Babur felt convinced after his interaction with Guru Nanak, That the latter had really an intimate relationship with God. Since there existed no distinction between God and Guru Nanak, He must seek his blessings for getting a sovereignty over India. (43)
lines: Babur felt convinced after his interaction with Guru Nanak,
That the latter had really an intimate relationship with God.
Since there existed no distinction between God and Guru Nanak,
He must seek his blessings for getting a sovereignty over India.

blocks.text: If, God willing, the Guru Nanak answered his prayers, All his dreams and aspirations will get materialized. If, God forbid, Guru Nanak declined his prayers, He would not lose anything substantial of his own. (44)
lines: If,
God willing, the Guru Nanak answered his prayers,
All his dreams and aspirations will get materialized.
If,
God forbid,
Guru Nanak declined his prayers,
He would not lose anything substantial of his own.

blocks.text: Why should he poison his future through his insolence, Instead, why should he not cultivate polite conversation? After this, folding his hands in supplication, Babur put forth, His dire necessity in words couched in politeness. (45)
lines: Why should he poison his future through his insolence,
Instead, why should he not cultivate polite conversation?
After this, folding his hands in supplication,
Babur put forth,
His dire necessity in words couched in politeness.

blocks.text: Prostrating at the lotus feet of Divine Guru Nanak, Babur begged for his aspirations to be fulfilled, Acknowledging Guru Nanak as the great Hindu prophet, He had sought the Guru's blessings in his dire need. (46)
lines: Prostrating at the lotus feet of Divine Guru Nanak,
Babur begged for his aspirations to be fulfilled,
Acknowledging Guru Nanak as the great Hindu prophet,
He had sought the Guru's blessings in his dire need.

blocks.text: Dohra:

Acknowledging Guru Nanak to be as great as he had heard, Babur declared the Guru as the greatest among spiritual prophets. Admitting that after having a glimpse of the Divine Guru, He felt assured of Guru Nanak's Divine attributes. (47)
lines: Acknowledging Guru Nanak to be as great as he had heard,
Babur declared the Guru as the greatest among spiritual prophets.
Admitting that after having a glimpse of the Divine Guru,
He felt assured of Guru Nanak's Divine attributes.

blocks.text: Chaupai:

Finding the Guru as venerated as in narrations he had heard, Babur found the Guru spiritually Supreme after a through probe. Whatever divine attributes of the Guru had Daulat Khan narrated, Babur had observed and confirmed with his own eyes. (48)
lines: Finding the Guru as venerated as in narrations he had heard,
Babur found the Guru spiritually Supreme after a through probe.
Whatever divine attributes of the Guru had Daulat Khan narrated,
Babur had observed and confirmed with his own eyes.

blocks.text: The way the (Lodhi) Pathans had got the Guru's followers assassinated, Daulat Khan had narrated the whole account to Babur. Babur also knew about Guru's displeasure with the Lodhi Pathans, As well as the Guru's will to dispense with their rule over India. (49)
lines: The way the (Lodhi) Pathans had got the Guru's followers assassinated,
Daulat Khan had narrated the whole account to Babur.
Babur also knew about Guru's displeasure with the Lodhi Pathans,
As well as the Guru's will to dispense with their rule over India.

blocks.text: It was Guru's will to call the Mughals from Kabul4 , As the Guru, being omniscient and privy to the Divinee Will. Babur told the Guru that the former had arrived at Guru's bidding, As Daulat Khan would bear witness to what he said. (50)
lines: It was Guru's will to call the Mughals from Kabul4 ,
As the Guru, being omniscient and privy to the Divinee Will.
Babur told the Guru that the former had arrived at Guru's bidding,
As Daulat Khan would bear witness to what he said.

blocks.text: Since Daulat Khan had invited him (Babur) in the Guru's name, The Guru must protect and stand by his humble servant. Babur begged the Guru to make him occupy India's throne, Making his sovereign writ run over all the twenty-two states. (51)
lines: Since Daulat Khan had invited him (Babur) in the Guru's name,
The Guru must protect and stand by his humble servant.
Babur begged the Guru to make him occupy India's throne,
Making his sovereign writ run over all the twenty-two states.

blocks.text: Dohra:

Babur said he had approached Guru Nanak with a fond wish, That the great Guru be Babur's spiritual mentor. Babur begged for a sovereignty over the Indian throne, So that his writ might run over the twenty-two states. (52)
lines: Babur said he had approached Guru Nanak with a fond wish,
That the great Guru be Babur's spiritual mentor.
Babur begged for a sovereignty over the Indian throne,
So that his writ might run over the twenty-two states.

blocks.text: Chaupai:

Upon this Baba Nanak reminded the supplicating Babur, That the latter wished to be made a sovereign by Prophet Mohammad5 . Admitting that Prophet Mohammad being inaccessible, Babur expressed his inability to seek Prophet's (Mohammad's) blessings. (53)
lines: Upon this Baba Nanak reminded the supplicating Babur,
That the latter wished to be made a sovereign by Prophet Mohammad5 .
Admitting that Prophet Mohammad being inaccessible,
Babur expressed his inability to seek Prophet's (Mohammad's) blessings.

blocks.text: Since his prophet was inhabitant of the Divine Court, It was located across the seven skies (in heavens). How could Babur (a human being) reach that Divine abode, About which he had heard but never seen it with his eyes? (54)
lines: Since his prophet was inhabitant of the Divine Court,
It was located across the seven skies (in heavens).
How could Babur (a human being) reach that Divine abode,
About which he had heard but never seen it with his eyes?

blocks.text: The Guru reminded Babur that he had boasted of being an emperor, Whose writ ran over half of humanity on the earth. How could he not reach his Islamic Prophet Mohammad, As he boasted of having the powers of five spiritual prophets? (55)
lines: The Guru reminded Babur that he had boasted of being an emperor,
Whose writ ran over half of humanity on the earth.
How could he not reach his Islamic Prophet Mohammad,
As he boasted of having the powers of five spiritual prophets?

blocks.text: Promising Babur to enable him to reach his prophet, The Guru directed Babur to seek sovereignty from his own prophet. Babur should reach the Divine Court in his prophet's company, Where his prophet would get a written sanction for his sovereignty. (56)
lines: Promising Babur to enable him to reach his prophet,
The Guru directed Babur to seek sovereignty from his own prophet.
Babur should reach the Divine Court in his prophet's company,
Where his prophet would get a written sanction for his sovereignty.

blocks.text: Dohra:

Hearing this, Babur bent on his knees in thankfulness, Begging Guru Nanak to enable him to have a glimpse of his own prophet. Being extremely confident of his prophet's divine powers, Babur was sure of getting India's sovereignty sanctioned. (57)
lines: Hearing this,
Babur bent on his knees in thankfulness,
Begging Guru Nanak to enable him to have a glimpse of his own prophet.
Being extremely confident of his prophet's divine powers,
Babur was sure of getting India's sovereignty sanctioned.

blocks.text: Chaupai:

Thereafter, Satguru Guru Nanak directed the Mughal emperor, That Guru's staff would lead Babur to the Divine court. Thereafter handing over his staff to the emperor Babur, Guru Nanak instructed Babur to sit on the ground in front of the staff. (58)
lines: Thereafter,
Satguru Guru Nanak directed the Mughal emperor,
That Guru's staff would lead Babur to the Divine court.
Thereafter handing over his staff to the emperor Babur,
Guru Nanak instructed Babur to sit on the ground in front of the staff.

blocks.text: With burning jos-sticks and a lamp, he should prostrate before the staff, After which it would take Babur wherever he wished to go. With the continuous recitation of God's holy Name 'Satnam', He could reach anywhere he wished to reach. (59)
lines: With burning jos-sticks and a lamp, he should prostrate before the staff,
After which it would take Babur wherever he wished to go.
With the continuous recitation of God's holy Name 'Satnam',
He could reach anywhere he wished to reach.

blocks.text: The Guru's staff would take Babur and his prophet to heaven, Where nobody would stop their entry into the Divine Court. The same Divine Court was it where prophet once had gone, But was made to return the same moment to his abode. (60)
lines: The Guru's staff would take Babur and his prophet to heaven,
Where nobody would stop their entry into the Divine Court.
The same Divine Court was it where prophet once had gone,
But was made to return the same moment to his abode.

blocks.text: With Guru's staff with them, they could stay there for many hours, While his prophet could converse with God for long. Staying there in the Divine Court for a longer spell, He and his prophet could seek whatever they wished. (61)
lines: With Guru's staff with them, they could stay there for many hours,
While his prophet could converse with God for long.
Staying there in the Divine Court for a longer spell,
He and his prophet could seek whatever they wished.

blocks.text: Dohra:

With a respectful bow did Babur depart from Guru Nanak, Wondering at heart at the promised great miracle. Following the Guru's instructions about invocation, Babur departed after holding the Guru's staff. (62)
lines: With a respectful bow did Babur depart from Guru Nanak,
Wondering at heart at the promised great miracle.
Following the Guru's instructions about invocation,
Babur departed after holding the Guru's staff.

blocks.text: Chaupai:

The moment Babur performed the proffered incantations, The Guru's staff took him on a flight the same moment. Flying across the seven skies with the Guru's staff, Babur reached the exclusive territory of the Divine Court. (63)
lines: The moment Babur performed the proffered incantations,
The Guru's staff took him on a flight the same moment.
Flying across the seven skies with the Guru's staff,
Babur reached the exclusive territory of the Divine Court.

blocks.text: He found the Divine Court bolted and barred from inside, Which did not open even at the approach of prophet Mohammad. But the moment Babur recited the Guru's word "Satnam", In an instant opened all the doors that were barred and locked. (64)
lines: He found the Divine Court bolted and barred from inside,
Which did not open even at the approach of prophet Mohammad.
But the moment Babur recited the Guru's word "Satnam",
In an instant opened all the doors that were barred and locked.

blocks.text: Babur witnessed Guru Nanak's standard fluttering in heavens, And heard spiritual hymns being recited from the holy books. Spiritual melodies were being recited to the accompaniment of music, Filling the whole environment with a spiritual ambience. (65)
lines: Babur witnessed Guru Nanak's standard fluttering in heavens,
And heard spiritual hymns being recited from the holy books.
Spiritual melodies were being recited to the accompaniment of music,
Filling the whole environment with a spiritual ambience.

blocks.text: Dohra:

Thus, Babur saw with his own eyes after reaching there, Guru Nanak's standard fluttering inside the Divine Court. Observing Nanak's standard fluttering at the entrance, Babur had a glimpse of God seated on the Divine seat. (66)
lines: Thus,
Babur saw with his own eyes after reaching there,
Guru Nanak's standard fluttering inside the Divine Court.
Observing Nanak's standard fluttering at the entrance,
Babur had a glimpse of God seated on the Divine seat.

blocks.text: Sparkling as the crystal waters of the scared Ganges, Guru Nanak's standard also emitted dark cloud like hues. Its saffron cloth fluttered as majestically as, If a spark of lightening had flitted across its surface. (67)
lines: Sparkling as the crystal waters of the scared Ganges,
Guru Nanak's standard also emitted dark cloud like hues.
Its saffron cloth fluttered as majestically as,
If a spark of lightening had flitted across its surface.

blocks.text: Chaupai:

The Guru's staff took Babur around Guru's meditational centre, Where several saints and sages sat cross-legged in meditation. So many spiritual supremos sat spell-bound unconcerned, Although several temporal and spiritual deities hovered around them. (68)
lines: The Guru's staff took Babur around Guru's meditational centre,
Where several saints and sages sat cross-legged in meditation.
So many spiritual supremos sat spell-bound unconcerned,
Although several temporal and spiritual deities hovered around them.

blocks.text: Dohra:

The Divine Court had, on its premises, five mythological trees6 , Bearing the names of Parjat, Kalap Birchh, Santaan, Harichandan and Mandhar. Besides, there were other trees laden with flowers and fruit, As well as the mythical cows of the Kamdhen7 breed. (69)
lines: The Divine Court had, on its premises, five mythological trees6 ,
Bearing the names of Parjat,
Kalap Birchh,
Santaan,
Harichandan and Mandhar.
Besides, there were other trees laden with flowers and fruit,
As well as the mythical cows of the Kamdhen7 breed.

blocks.text: Chaupai:

With rare "Chinta Mani8 " stones were the walls of Divine Court built, With fragrant golden paint were these rare walls painted. With "Vaduraya"9 stones were pillars of Divine Court erected, With the fragrant Sandalwood was its majestic roof inlaid. (70)
lines: With rare "Chinta Mani8 " stones were the walls of Divine Court built,
With fragrant golden paint were these rare walls painted.
With "Vaduraya"9 stones were pillars of Divine Court erected,
With the fragrant Sandalwood was its majestic roof inlaid.

blocks.text: With corals were the doors of the Divine Court made, With designs on the philosopher's stone were these doors carved. After taking Babur on a round of the Divine Court, The Guru's staff brought him back to the Divine entrance. (71)
lines: With corals were the doors of the Divine Court made,
With designs on the philosopher's stone were these doors carved.
After taking Babur on a round of the Divine Court,
The Guru's staff brought him back to the Divine entrance.

blocks.text: Thereafter taking Babur to his (Islamic) prophet's enclosure, The Guru's staff showed him the Muslim cleric reciting an Islamic prayer. Babur was shown a glimpse of his Prophet's standard, Which had not been dyed in blue for a long time. (72)
lines: Thereafter taking Babur to his (Islamic) prophet's enclosure,
The Guru's staff showed him the Muslim cleric reciting an Islamic prayer.
Babur was shown a glimpse of his Prophet's standard,
Which had not been dyed in blue for a long time.

blocks.text: There was situated a mosque, place of Muslim worship, That was designed as per Prophet's own tradition. As Babur had a glimpse of his spiritual prophet Mohammad, He started prostrating and supplicating before him. (73)
lines: There was situated a mosque, place of Muslim worship,
That was designed as per Prophet's own tradition.
As Babur had a glimpse of his spiritual prophet Mohammad,
He started prostrating and supplicating before him.

blocks.text: Prophet Mohammad himself was seen praying to God, Entreating the Divine Lord to accept his supplication. Behind him stood his foremost intimate devout followers10, Followed by thousands of other Muslims spiritual saints. (74)
lines: Prophet Mohammad himself was seen praying to God,
Entreating the Divine Lord to accept his supplication.
Behind him stood his foremost intimate devout followers10,
Followed by thousands of other Muslims spiritual saints.

blocks.text: Directing Babur to stand in the queue at the back, The Guru's staff informed Prophet Mohammad about Babur's visit. Summoning Babur from the back to his own proximity, Prophet Mohammad asked Babur about the purpose of his visit. (75)
lines: Directing Babur to stand in the queue at the back,
The Guru's staff informed Prophet Mohammad about Babur's visit.
Summoning Babur from the back to his own proximity,
Prophet Mohammad asked Babur about the purpose of his visit.

blocks.text: Babur pleaded to be blessed with a sovereignty over India, So that his writ might run over the twenty-two Indian provinces. Instantly did Prophet Mohammad reject Babur's plea with a remark, That He had no divine sanction for granting a sovereignty over India. (76)
lines: Babur pleaded to be blessed with a sovereignty over India,
So that his writ might run over the twenty-two Indian provinces.
Instantly did Prophet Mohammad reject Babur's plea with a remark,
That He had no divine sanction for granting a sovereignty over India.

blocks.text: Sovereignty of India being the sole prerogative of Guru Nanak, Babur should have no expectations from his prophet about it. (77)
lines: Sovereignty of India being the sole prerogative of Guru Nanak,
Babur should have no expectations from his prophet about it.

blocks.text: Sortha:

Mohammad told Babur India's sovereignty being Guru Nanak's prerogative, The former had no jurisdiction over India's sovereignty. He advised Babur to get his cherished desire fulfilled from Guru Nanak, By whatever modes of supplication he deemed fit to appease Nanak. (78)
lines: Mohammad told Babur India's sovereignty being Guru Nanak's prerogative,
The former had no jurisdiction over India's sovereignty.
He advised Babur to get his cherished desire fulfilled from Guru Nanak,
By whatever modes of supplication he deemed fit to appease Nanak.

blocks.text: Chaupai:

The Guru's staff which brought him to the heavens, His blessings should Babur invoke to get sovereignty. Sovereignty over India not being in his jurisdiction, The prophet had powers to grant sovereignty over Khorasan alone. (79)
lines: The Guru's staff which brought him to the heavens,
His blessings should Babur invoke to get sovereignty.
Sovereignty over India not being in his jurisdiction,
The prophet had powers to grant sovereignty over Khorasan alone.

blocks.text: He had already granted Khorasan's sovereignty to Taimurlang" , Whose legal heirs were entitled to inherit his legacy. Thereafter, whatever further appeals Babur made, Those were declined forthwith by Prophet Mohammad. (80)
lines: He had already granted Khorasan's sovereignty to Taimurlang" ,
Whose legal heirs were entitled to inherit his legacy.
Thereafter, whatever further appeals Babur made,
Those were declined forthwith by Prophet Mohammad.

blocks.text: Feeling frustrated returned Babur empty handed, Landing at his camp with the grace of the Guru's staff. So frustrated and listless had Babur felt, As if his mortal frame had broke in twain. (81)
lines: Feeling frustrated returned Babur empty handed,
Landing at his camp with the grace of the Guru's staff.
So frustrated and listless had Babur felt,
As if his mortal frame had broke in twain.

blocks.text: Babur fainted on his arrival at his army camp, So severely was he struck with a sense of remorse. He recalled the prophetic words of his own minister, Who had warned him about the presence of a great Hindu prophet. (82)
lines: Babur fainted on his arrival at his army camp,
So severely was he struck with a sense of remorse.
He recalled the prophetic words of his own minister,
Who had warned him about the presence of a great Hindu prophet.

blocks.text: Dohra:

Being equally scared of returning to his Islamic prophet, As well as going ahead with an appeal to Guru Nanak, Was Babur really caught on the horns of a dilemma, As that of a snake which fails either to swallow or vomit out a poisonous lizard. (83)
lines: Being equally scared of returning to his Islamic prophet,
As well as going ahead with an appeal to Guru Nanak,
Was Babur really caught on the horns of a dilemma,
As that of a snake which fails either to swallow or vomit out a poisonous lizard.

blocks.text: Chaupai:

With Babur's whole frame being in convulsions with fear, Was he severely struck with a rising wave of doubts. His Islamic prophet having rejected his pleas, He had thrown Babur at the mercy of a Hindu prophet. (84)
lines: With Babur's whole frame being in convulsions with fear,
Was he severely struck with a rising wave of doubts.
His Islamic prophet having rejected his pleas,
He had thrown Babur at the mercy of a Hindu prophet.

blocks.text: Whom should he look up to in his hour of dire need, Whom should he supplicate before for his dream fulfilment? Having been caught in the whirlwind of life, His own prophet had left him in the lurch. (85)
lines: Whom should he look up to in his hour of dire need,
Whom should he supplicate before for his dream fulfilment?
Having been caught in the whirlwind of life,
His own prophet had left him in the lurch.

blocks.text: How could his ship of life reach its shore without a mariner, Whom should he pray for a survival from this ordeal? Being burdened with such depressing thoughts, Did Babur keep oscillating between hope and fear. (86)
lines: How could his ship of life reach its shore without a mariner,
Whom should he pray for a survival from this ordeal?
Being burdened with such depressing thoughts,
Did Babur keep oscillating between hope and fear.

blocks.text: Dohra:

Thereafter a thought came to Babur's mind, Which provided a great solace to him. He recalled how even his own spiritual prophet Mohammad, Had confirmed that Nanak alone was the only prophet in India. (87)
lines: Thereafter a thought came to Babur's mind,
Which provided a great solace to him.
He recalled how even his own spiritual prophet Mohammad,
Had confirmed that Nanak alone was the only prophet in India.

blocks.text: Chaupai:
Thereupon, a thought overtook Babur's mind, That he should seek blessings of Guru Nanak. Nanak being the greatest among the spiritual prophets, Who else could provide an enduring support? (88)
lines: Thereupon, a thought overtook Babur's mind,
That he should seek blessings of Guru Nanak.
Nanak being the greatest among the spiritual prophets,
Who else could provide an enduring support?

blocks.text: Summoning Daulat Khan the same moment, Babur accused the latter of landing him in trouble. He, being caught badly in the life's whirlwinds, Daulat must plead before the Guru to be Babur's saviour. (89)
lines: Summoning Daulat Khan the same moment,
Babur accused the latter of landing him in trouble.
He, being caught badly in the life's whirlwinds,
Daulat must plead before the Guru to be Babur's saviour.

blocks.text: Taking Babur along, did Daulat Khan approach the Guru, With folded hands, did they bow before the Guru. Professing to be the most humble slave of the Guru, Babur pleaded before the Guru for his dream to be fulfilled. (90)
lines: Taking Babur along, did Daulat Khan approach the Guru,
With folded hands, did they bow before the Guru.
Professing to be the most humble slave of the Guru,
Babur pleaded before the Guru for his dream to be fulfilled.

blocks.text: Dohra:

Narrating whatever he had observed at the Divine Court, Babur put forth his observations before Guru Nanak. Being omniscient about what happened here and there, The Guru gave a faint smile and kept his cool. (91)
lines: Narrating whatever he had observed at the Divine Court,
Babur put forth his observations before Guru Nanak.
Being omniscient about what happened here and there,
The Guru gave a faint smile and kept his cool.

blocks.text: Chaupai:

Thereafter (struck with wonder and awe), remarked Babur, Nobody could ever gauge the spiritual profundity of Guru Nanak. The Guru, being the (dearest) son of God Divine, He alone could match the Divine in attributes Divine. (92)
lines: Thereafter (struck with wonder and awe), remarked Babur,
Nobody could ever gauge the spiritual profundity of Guru Nanak.
The Guru, being the (dearest) son of God Divine,
He alone could match the Divine in attributes Divine.

blocks.text: Both God and Guru Nanak being inseparable, The Guru's will prevailed in every phenomenal occurring. Infinite was the limit of Guru Nanak's blessings, As his will was the cause behind every happening. (93)
lines: Both God and Guru Nanak being inseparable,
The Guru's will prevailed in every phenomenal occurring.
Infinite was the limit of Guru Nanak's blessings,
As his will was the cause behind every happening.

blocks.text: Being himself the Divine and merciful like Him, Guru Nanak was the creator and the compassionate. He, being both the prophet and the spiritual guide, Impossible was it to plumb the depth of the Guru's mystique. (94)
lines: Being himself the Divine and merciful like Him,
Guru Nanak was the creator and the compassionate.
He, being both the prophet and the spiritual guide,
Impossible was it to plumb the depth of the Guru's mystique.

blocks.text: Dohra:

Claiming to repose complete faith in Nanak's Divinity, Had Babur surrendered to Daulat Khan's proposal. Imploring the Guru to protect his (Babur 's) honour, Let the Guru deal with him (Babur) as he willed. (95)
lines: Claiming to repose complete faith in Nanak's Divinity,
Had Babur surrendered to Daulat Khan's proposal.
Imploring the Guru to protect his (Babur 's) honour,
Let the Guru deal with him (Babur) as he willed.

blocks.text: Chaupai:

Taking pity on Babur after hearing his entreaties, The Guru asked him to bring forth his bag of cannabis. Hearing Guru's willingness to shower his blessings, Babur opened his bag full of of cannabis leaves postehate. (96)
lines: Taking pity on Babur after hearing his entreaties,
The Guru asked him to bring forth his bag of cannabis.
Hearing Guru's willingness to shower his blessings,
Babur opened his bag full of of cannabis leaves postehate.

blocks.text: As the Guru put seven handfuls of cannabis leaves into Babaur's lap, The Guru turned the cannabis bag upside down. With the giving of seven handfuls of cannabis thus, The Guru blessed Babur with sovereignty upto his seven dynasties. (97)
lines: As the Guru put seven handfuls of cannabis leaves into Babaur's lap,
The Guru turned the cannabis bag upside down.
With the giving of seven handfuls of cannabis thus,
The Guru blessed Babur with sovereignty upto his seven dynasties.

blocks.text: Looking at the Cannabis leaves lying on the ground, The Guru was at liberty to take back his blessings again. Even the sovereignty already granted to the seven dynasties of Babur, The Guru would take it back at an appropriate moment. (98)
lines: Looking at the Cannabis leaves lying on the ground,
The Guru was at liberty to take back his blessings again.
Even the sovereignty already granted to the seven dynasties of Babur,
The Guru would take it back at an appropriate moment.

blocks.text: Dohra:

Thus, the Guru, in a moment of carefree abandon, Vested Babur with India's sovereignty for a pittance. Little realizing that this blessing would recoil upon his own house, Much as Lord Shiva's blessing to Demon Bhasmantar12 had recoiled. (99)
lines: Thus, the Guru, in a moment of carefree abandon,
Vested Babur with India's sovereignty for a pittance.
Little realizing that this blessing would recoil upon his own house,
Much as Lord Shiva's blessing to Demon Bhasmantar12 had recoiled.

blocks.text: Sortha:

When the Guru addressed these words to Babur that, He had conferred India's sovereignty on Babur for a pittance. The Guru had also made a commitment at that moment, That He would be entitled to revoke his blessings. (100)
lines: When the Guru addressed these words to Babur that,
He had conferred India's sovereignty on Babur for a pittance.
The Guru had also made a commitment at that moment,
That He would be entitled to revoke his blessings.

blocks.text: Thereafter, Satguru Guru Nanak made it absolutely clear, Drawing the attention of emperor Babur to his words. The Guru would snatch India's sovereignty perforce, When Babur would no longer be present on the scene. (101)
lines: Thereafter,
Satguru Guru Nanak made it absolutely clear,
Drawing the attention of emperor Babur to his words.
The Guru would snatch India's sovereignty perforce,
When Babur would no longer be present on the scene.

blocks.text: Ardil:

Hearing this conditional grant of sovereignty by Guru Nanak, Babur addressed the Guru in the following vein: Taking back a boon after it had been granted, Amounted to going back on one's own words. It was as ignominious to withdraw a favour granted, As one licked one's own spittle. It was dishonour to take back a granted boon, As it brought a great disgrace to the giver. (102)
lines: Hearing this conditional grant of sovereignty by Guru Nanak,
Babur addressed the Guru in the following vein: Taking back a boon after it had been granted,
Amounted to going back on one's own words.
It was as ignominious to withdraw a favour granted,
As one licked one's own spittle.
It was dishonour to take back a granted boon,
As it brought a great disgrace to the giver.

blocks.text: Dohra:

Thereupon, Guru Nanak reminded (the arguing) Babur, That favours granted were withdrawn under certain conditions. Sometime the recipient, receiving a boon gratis, Proved unworthy of preserving such a boon. (103)
lines: Thereupon,
Guru Nanak reminded (the arguing) Babur,
That favours granted were withdrawn under certain conditions.
Sometime the recipient, receiving a boon gratis,
Proved unworthy of preserving such a boon.

blocks.text: Chhand:

Such a boon Divine in return for nothing, Had Mansoor13 (an Iraqui Sufi Saint) acquired. Failing to contain its spiritual worth in himself, The boon cost (that unfortunate saint) his life. Being as evanescent as the highly volatile camphor, It is difficult to contain a boon received gratis. It disappears as instantly as camphor exposed to fire, Leaving its beneficiary devoid of its blessings. (104)
lines: Such a boon Divine in return for nothing,
Had Mansoor13 (an Iraqui Sufi Saint) acquired.
Failing to contain its spiritual worth in himself,
The boon cost (that unfortunate saint) his life.
Being as evanescent as the highly volatile camphor,
It is difficult to contain a boon received gratis.
It disappears as instantly as camphor exposed to fire,
Leaving its beneficiary devoid of its blessings.

blocks.text: Dohra:

Thereupon, Guru Nanak told Babur in a prophetic vein, That Babur's House would forget about Guru's blessings. As his successors would persecute Guru's successors, The Guru's Will would revoke his blessed sovereignty bestowed on Mughals. (105)
lines: Thereupon,
Guru Nanak told Babur in a prophetic vein,
That Babur's House would forget about Guru's blessings.
As his successors would persecute Guru's successors,
The Guru's Will would revoke his blessed sovereignty bestowed on Mughals.

blocks.text: Chaupai:

Thereupon, with folded hands pleaded Babur before Guru Nanak, How could his progeny persecute the Guru's successors? With Babur's House holding Guru Nanak in high esteem, How could his successors dare to harm the Guru's House? (106)
lines: Thereupon, with folded hands pleaded Babur before Guru Nanak,
How could his progeny persecute the Guru's successors?
With Babur's House holding Guru Nanak in high esteem,
How could his successors dare to harm the Guru's House?

blocks.text: Hindustan's sovereignty being the monopoly of the Hindu prophets, Guru Nanak was supreme among those Divine prophets. Mughals having been made sovereign rulers by Guru Nanak, How could Mughals afford to turn against Nanak's House. (107)
lines: Hindustan's sovereignty being the monopoly of the Hindu prophets,
Guru Nanak was supreme among those Divine prophets.
Mughals having been made sovereign rulers by Guru Nanak,
How could Mughals afford to turn against Nanak's House.

blocks.text: Dohra:

The moment Babur's successors tyrannized Guru Nanak's dynasty, The Guru should take back India's sovereignty from Babur. It was on the basis of that solemn commitment, That Mughal's rule should extend beyond his seven dynasties. (108)
lines: The moment Babur's successors tyrannized Guru Nanak's dynasty,
The Guru should take back India's sovereignty from Babur.
It was on the basis of that solemn commitment,
That Mughal's rule should extend beyond his seven dynasties.

blocks.text: Chaupai:

With this agreement, the Guru conferred sovereignty on Babur, His first three dynasties did honour this solemn commitment. Babur, being succeeded by his own son Himanyun to the throne, Akbar, being born to Himanyun, did succeed him further. (109)
lines: With this agreement, the Guru conferred sovereignty on Babur,
His first three dynasties did honour this solemn commitment.
Babur, being succeeded by his own son Himanyun to the throne,
Akbar, being born to Himanyun, did succeed him further.

blocks.text: These three successors, holding Nanak's House in very high esteem, Never uttered a single word against the Guru's glory. As the fourth Mughal emperor Jahangir ascended to India's throne, He became a captive in the hands of bigoted Muslim clerics. (110)
lines: These three successors, holding Nanak's House in very high esteem,
Never uttered a single word against the Guru's glory.
As the fourth Mughal emperor Jahangir ascended to India's throne,
He became a captive in the hands of bigoted Muslim clerics.

blocks.text: These clerics, having fell foul of (fifth Sikh Guru) Guru Arjun, Laid the whole blame (for Guru Arjun's execution) on a Kashtriya14 courtier. The fifth Mughal emperor in dynastic line being Shah Jahan, He converted many Hindus into Islam (under duress). (Ill) Auranzeb, being the sixth in the Mughal dynasty, He entered into a big strife with the Sikh Gurus. Summoning the infant Sikh Guru Harkrishan (to Delhi), The Guru shed his mortal frame after blaming Aurangzeb. (112)
lines: These clerics, having fell foul of (fifth Sikh Guru) Guru Arjun,
Laid the whole blame (for Guru Arjun's execution) on a Kashtriya14 courtier.
The fifth Mughal emperor in dynastic line being Shah Jahan,
He converted many Hindus into Islam (under duress).
(Ill) Auranzeb, being the sixth in the Mughal dynasty,
He entered into a big strife with the Sikh Gurus.
Summoning the infant Sikh Guru Harkrishan (to Delhi),
The Guru shed his mortal frame after blaming Aurangzeb.

blocks.text: Dohra:

Committing innumerable atrocities on Guru's House, Aurangzeb executed (the ninth Sikh Guru) Guru Tegh Bahadur, The blame squarely came to be laid on Aurangeb's head, For the execution of Guru Tegh Bahadur's four grandsons. (113)
lines: Committing innumerable atrocities on Guru's House,
Aurangzeb executed (the ninth Sikh Guru) Guru Tegh Bahadur,
The blame squarely came to be laid on Aurangeb's head,
For the execution of Guru Tegh Bahadur's four grandsons.

blocks.text: Chaupai:

Guru Gobind Singh, having contemplated over Guru Nanak's prophecy, Reckoned that Mughal dynasty would last only for one generation. Contemplating to sacrifice his life to get the Mughals damned, Guru Gobind resolved to adopt this course. (114)
lines: Guru Gobind Singh, having contemplated over Guru Nanak's prophecy,
Reckoned that Mughal dynasty would last only for one generation.
Contemplating to sacrifice his life to get the Mughals damned,
Guru Gobind resolved to adopt this course.

blocks.text: Thus fulfilling his vow with his own supreme sacrifice, The Mughal's seven generations' dynastic rule came to an end. Suffering persecution for his own prophetic words of promise, The Sikh Gurus' sacrificed themselves to uphold Guru Nanak's words. (115)
lines: Thus fulfilling his vow with his own supreme sacrifice,
The Mughal's seven generations' dynastic rule came to an end.
Suffering persecution for his own prophetic words of promise,
The Sikh Gurus' sacrificed themselves to uphold Guru Nanak's words.

blocks.text: Dohra:

Thus, did the Mughals having committed a breach of trust, Went back from their vows made to Guru Nanak. Throwing all their solemn pledges to the winds, They claimed having attained sovereignty on their own. (116)
lines: Thus, did the Mughals having committed a breach of trust,
Went back from their vows made to Guru Nanak.
Throwing all their solemn pledges to the winds,
They claimed having attained sovereignty on their own.

blocks.text: Chaupai:

Claiming themselves to be powerful and autonomous, They claimed to have decimated India's Hindus. Claiming their spiritual prophet (Mohammad) to be closest to God, They rejected Hindu prophets' (the Gurus) proximity to God. (117)
lines: Claiming themselves to be powerful and autonomous,
They claimed to have decimated India's Hindus.
Claiming their spiritual prophet (Mohammad) to be closest to God,
They rejected Hindu prophets' (the Gurus) proximity to God.

blocks.text: Dohra:

Such was the extent of ignorance and willful disobedience, Into which had the Mughal emperors been engulfed. Being hynotised by the glib talk of the bigoted Muslim clerics, The Mughal rulers violated all their solemn commitments. (118)
lines: Such was the extent of ignorance and willful disobedience,
Into which had the Mughal emperors been engulfed.
Being hynotised by the glib talk of the bigoted Muslim clerics,
The Mughal rulers violated all their solemn commitments.
